Mario Cipollini's domestic abuse case ends, having exceeded the statute of limitations

Mario Cipollini has announced on Instagram that he is "a citizen with a completely clean criminal record", following the annulment of his 2022 conviction for domestic abuse and stalking.

The former Italian sprinter was facing a three-year prison term after being found guilty of domestic mistreatment, stalking, bodily harm and threats against his ex-wife Sabrina Landucci, in a case that had dragged on since 2017 and was frequently beset by delays and appeals.

Those appeals continued post-conviction, with Cipollini's lawyers challenging the sentencing court's version of events by suggesting discrepancies with the timeline of the alleged incidents. The appeals court then ran out of time to hear this latest challenge, with the implication that, Cipollini says, "all charges became time-barred under the statute of limitations".

Cipollini's Instagram post takes a somewhat celebratory tone, and says that "I accept this outcome with complete peace of mind, with the only regret being that I was drawn into a legal proceeding that perhaps should never have begun in the first place." His post does not mention that he paid around ~€100,000 to Landucci in an out-of-court settlement, and that she has never withdrawn the complaints she initially made.

LPGA Tour Q-Series: Megan Khang secures tour card for 2027 as Megha Ganne wins final qualifying stage

The top-25 finishers and ties at the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying stage have been awarded LPGA Tour status for 2027; Megha Ganne won the event outright, while Megan Khang - part of Team USA for the past five Solheim Cups - is one of 27 players to claim a tour card for next season

Monday 23 November 2026 23:16, UK

Megha Ganne won the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying stage as 27 tour cards were claimed for the 2027 season, with five-time USA Solheim Cup team member Megan Khang among those successful.

Khang - part of Team USA for the past five Solheim Cups - is returning to the LPGA Tour, on which she's made 259 starts since 2016, winning the 2023 CPKC Women's Open.

The top-25 finishers and ties at the conclusion of the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying were awarded LPGA Tour status for next year.

American Ganne won the final stage outright on 23 under, one shot clear of Shannon Tan and Julia Gregg in a tie for second. Min Sun7 Kim was fourth on 21 under and Xiaowen Yin one further back in fifth.

Ganne, the 2025 US Amateur champion, had actually already secured her 2027 LPGA Tour status by entering the week by finishing 11-15 on the Epson Tour.

Gregg, who finished in a share of second, has never previously had a start on the LPGA Tour.

"It feels unreal," the 25-year-old American said after clinching her place. "It's been my dream since I was four years old to play on the LPGA and now that I finally did it."

The WTGL season continues on Wednesday when Lottie Woad's Boston Common chase their first win of the campaign against Charley Hull's Atlanta Drive GC. Live coverage begins on Wednesday from 1am on Sky Sports Golf.

item.title: Why sustained strength training makes you a better cyclist
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Almost every cyclist agrees that strength training matters, that is, until they actually step into a gym and have to turn theory into practice. While some worry about gaining weight and plenty of others dread the soreness that can ruin a week of riding, for many, it is easy to feel lost at sea amid flashy but confusing Instagram clips, unfamiliar gym equipment, and conflicting advice.

The problem isn’t a lack of information – far from it. It’s that there’s too much, with so much of it poorly contextualised, especially for cyclists. As Matt Smith, founder of Ride Strong and strength coach to athletes including Kate Courtney and Christopher Blevins, puts it: “We’re in this age of mass information now, and the goal with coaches is to create better discretion to filter the noise and create some coherent through-lines so athletes can make well-founded decisions.”

While training on the bike feels familiar and directly beneficial, swapping a ride for a gym session can feel like a gamble. Most of us feel confident in our understanding of interval training, endurance rides, and how rest days fit into the mix. As a result, mistakes from on-bike training tend to self-correct before they become problematic (not always, of course). The gym, by contrast, feels riskier, with less obvious benefits and a higher risk of injuries and setbacks if done incorrectly.

But effective strength training for cyclists doesn’t have to be complicated, and it likely requires less time than you envision. In reality, strength training rests on a few simple principles, and when approached this way, adding some consistent strength sessions to your training can elevate your riding rather than hinder it.

What strength training is actually for (and what it isn’t)

One of the biggest mistakes made when adding gym work is assuming it’s purely about increasing maximal strength. Smith frames it more broadly: “The way that I view gym training or off-bike training in general is general athletic development,” he said. Raw strength is part of the picture, but far from the whole thing. He also advises athletes to remember that strength work is there to serve the bigger goal of boosting performance on the bike. “Gym training creates the canvas for you to paint on with the bike,” Smith explained. It is not the painting.”

This approach develops a broader athletic profile, including balance, muscular endurance, symmetry, explosivity, and injury resistance. “There are all these different attributes of an athlete that we’re trying to address in a strength training program,” he said. In that sense, Smith considers the simple term “strength training” to be misleading: “It’s not really how I consider gym work,” he added.

That matters because the act of cycling is an incredibly specific movement pattern. Hundreds of hours in the saddle may develop your FTP and aerobic capacity, but they do little for overall athleticism. That's where strength training can help, Smith believes.

item.title: Kansas City Current play spoiler to win first NWSL championship
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

The Kansas City Current defeated Washington Spirit 2-1 in a chippy affair on a less-than-ideal pitch in the nation’s capital to win their first league title. The match was marked by its physicality as the Current prevailed with a disciplined approach that hinged on disruption.

Kansas City Current play spoiler to win first NWSL championship

Vanessa DiBernardo and Debinha were on the scoresheet in a hostile road atmosphere.

Kansas City had to come up with a plan to nullify Spirit striker Clara Luvanga, who had recorded six goal contributions in the four games leading up to the final. At first, things started off a little shaky for the visiting side, as Luvanga pressured Kansas City center back Gabrielle Robinson into giving up an early corner. However, before she got substituted in the 74th minute, Luvanga managed her fewest total touches in the penalty area in a single game since she cemented a place in Washington’s starting XI—a testament to the success of the Current’s strategy.

The game was physical, highlighted by five fouls committed in the first five minutes of the game. Spirit forward Trinity Rodman had to receive treatment on the field following a hard tackle from Kansas City right back Laney Rouse. When asked whether the action early on set the tone for the game, Rodman joked, “Well, in the sense that it hurt really bad, yeah.” She continued on to say that, “you’re taught to make the first hit, so credit to them because I wish I was the one that put her on the ground.”

Rodman didn’t quite look the same following the tackle. Her movements were slow and stiff for the most part, but she still found it in herself to be explosive when a big opportunity arose, contributing to big chances for her teammates. In fact, both of Luvanga’s two touches in the attacking penalty area came from Rodman creating a chance for her.

However, Rodman’s slightly limited range of motion also posed problems for her team. In particular, she uncharacteristically gave possession away to Temwa Chawinga in the 11th minute. Fortunately for Rodman, goalkeeper Sandy MacIver made a massive save to keep things level.

The first half retained a high level of physicality, smashing the previous record for the most fouls in the first half of an NWSL championship match with 19 between the two teams.

Nine minutes into the second half, midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo scored a goal straight from a corner kick, eventually earning herself championship MVP honors. At 34 years old, DiBernardo briefly became the oldest player to score in an NWSL Championship match before her short-lived record was broken by teammate Debinha in stoppage time.

The Brazilian received the ball in her own half and sprinted to the opposing goal, beating MacIver in the process to cement the trophy for Kansas City. In doing so, Debinha became the oldest goalscorer in an NWSL final.

Debinha’s goal ended up standing as the game-winner as Washington pulled one back in the ninth minute of second half stoppage time. Rodman secured a looping header towards the far post in a set piece situation and briefly reignited her team’s hopes for a championship.

Though, four minutes later the final whistle blew and the Kansas City Current were officially crowned NWSL champions for the first time in club history. “I walked into a really good team. There was a good culture built in, there were a lot of good pieces, and that was one of the reasons that lured me to the club,” Current head coach Chris Armas said after the game.

“I’m relying on these amazing people and players to help keep things steady but we have talent all along. We just had to get everyone back and healthy and then we knew we’d have a chance. The question was, ‘Will we have enough time?’ And we had time and they did the rest. We stayed steady. We have a great team and we peaked at the right time. And now they’re champions. We’ve been talking about being champions for a few months now and there it is.”

item.title: The Mets’ ridiculous Tarik Skubal contract is the last vestige of MLB’s old world
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

In the liminal space of the immediately pre-lockout MLB offseason, Tarik Skubal has conducted a contradictory orchestra. In signing a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets, he has managed to get both far more than he deserves and not as much as he should have. Let me explain.

The Mets’ ridiculous Tarik Skubal contract is the last vestige of MLB’s old world

How do you even judge the Tarik Skubal contract without knowing how it will count?

It’s a pretty terrible contract for the Mets, but we have no clue how terrible since we have no clue if there will be a salary cap, and even if there is, we have no clue how super contracts like Skubal’s will count against it. However, if this was just a normal year with no apocalyptic labor showdown coming over the horizon like a 200-foot tsunami ready to wipe multiple cities off the map, Skubal probably would have signed for far more. The Los Angeles Dodgers, apparently, did not even make him an offer — with the lockout coming on December 1, this may have been Skubal’s first, last and only offer.

If the Dodgers were out, then the Mets were bidding against … nobody. There are lots of fascinating reasons for why that is fascinating, so let’s get into all of them and decide whether Skubal’s deal is the prophet of doom or if we’re all going to be fine.

The MLB world stands on the precipice of an earth-shattering labor war that could cancel an entire season. From where I currently stand (and I change where I stand quite often to get better views), it looks like the result of all this will be the introduction of a salary cap, probably the most disruptive change to MLB’s competitive ecosystem in its history. To me, the owners have too much leverage to ultimately lose, and the MLB Players Association has too small a platform beyond essentially saying, “why are you guys being like this?”

Unless the owners somehow buckle, which I don’t believe they will, Tarik Skubal was the last major signing of the free market era and got the largest pitcher contract ever, both by total and annual value, blowing Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s deal completely out of the water and giving Steven Cohen one last moment to say he didn’t care about how much his team cost.

That’s a lie, of course, as Cohen is very much in league with the other owners to impose a cap on his players in order to skyrocket his franchise value and to share less money with those players. It’s the ultimate under-the-table conspiracy, in which MLB’s owners outwardly boast about trying to increase the quality of the sport while by far the greatest increase will come to the weight of their pockets. And they will cancel a season to do it, because the amount of money we’re talking about here is nuts.

The fact that Cohen just signed Skubal and is still pursuing a salary cap to make sure he can never do such a thing in the future speaks to the titanic strength of the owners’ position and why I see it as so likely that we will see a salary cap at the end of all this. Most people simply don’t understand that big market owners also want a cap because their earning potential spikes just the same, and that owners don’t think like fans — Cohen is happy to pay Skubal now to win goodwill from his fans for the next 10 years, while also stabbing his players in the back to secure yet more billions of dollars for himself and his family for the next quadrillion years.

The fact that the Mets and Dodgers always sign these big free agents continues to underscore how a salary cap would marginally improve baseball for many fans, especially those of small markets, but the cost of an entire season does not feel remotely worth those small improvements, especially since the primary beneficiaries are … uh, billionaires. I’m a bit of a broken record on that, but it’s the only rational position I have found in the cesspool of public broadsides and polemics.

Okay, what about the baseball side of things? Because Skubal’s $450 million and the many other super contracts of the free market era were signed before a cap was introduced, they will almost certainly not be counted simply against it. If a salary cap does emerge from this battle, contracts like Skubal’s and Juan Soto’s $765 million will probably have to be prorated somehow across whatever a maximum contract turns out to be in the new system. Otherwise, deferred money like with Shohei Ohtani’s contract would become rather silly, with the ghost of Ohtani counting $68 million against the Dodgers salary cap in 2043. Skubal will obviously receive the full value of that contract somehow, but nobody on earth knows how an eventual cap will distribute the payroll of the Mets and Dodgers, who have so much money committed for so long it might take a Nobel Prize in Economics to figure it out. So we shall just put that aside.

In a vacuum, then, it’s an awful contract. Unless your argument is that “there’s no cap, so it doesn’t matter, Steve Cohen has 25 gazillion dollars,” which I guess can just invalidate anything anyone could ever say … then it’s pretty inarguably a crazy contract for a 30-year-old pitcher who’s had three left elbow surgeries. Skubal is a remarkable player, probably the best pitcher in the world if everything is equal, but a hard $50 million per year for a pitcher until they’re 39 is one of those contracts you just know will be on a “worst contracts in MLB” list I’ll make in 2033.

In not-a-vacuum, the contract is a real risk. The fact that the Dodgers were unwilling to even engage with Skubal shows two things: first, how likely it actually is that we get a salary cap since the Dodgers were concerned about overextending their finances and second, that whatever that cap looks like could be rather punishing to the Mets and Dodgers who will be loaded with max contracts right off the rip. The Mets just signed an incredible player, yes, but we’re right on the edge of a Brave New World — there’s no way this contract ages well.…

Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree?

Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): If you watched the Brighton game and wondered how on earth Hull won it was because Konstantinos Tzolakis was in goal. An unbelievable performance with five or six top-class saves. Big moments, big personality, he has stepped up every time. He's been one of the players of the season - I know it's a bit too early to crown people but if it stopped now he has to be goalkeeper of the season.

James Hill (Bournemouth): He backed up getting into the England squad. Sometimes when people get called up they start to get above their stations but he didn't do that at all. He was in a really good state of form. A cheeky assist as well but defensively solid. He has been in my team a few times now - a centre-half who does his job without complaining.

Malick Thiaw (Newcastle): He divides opinion but he played really well and got his goal.

Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): Two goals against Everton and that was before the sending-off of James Tarkowski. Performed well again. Sneaky bargain buy of the century to be honest.

Noah Okafor (Leeds): Two goals again. Leeds battered Chelsea and made them look unbelievably average. Nobody has been talking about how sneaky good Leeds have been, some really big performances this season.

Jack Rudoni (Coventry): Two assists in a must-win game against Crystal Palace. He stepped up big, fair play to him.

Elliott Anderson (Manchester City): The only person who actually showed a pulse in this game. He got a goal and showed pace and showed he wanted to be there. He tried his best to win a game of football.

Luca Williams-Barnett (Tottenham): Young man, a with goal and an assist. He just gave Spurs a spark we haven't seen for probably six or seven years now. He gave them that spark instantly and fair play to De Zerbi for putting him in. All the money spent, who knew it would be a home-grown talent in their youth team who would step up and really get the Spurs fans excited.

Florian Wirtz (Liverpool): Unbelievable performance. He has had a bit of a purple patch since Jurgen Klopp has taken over Germany. Did really well in terms of finding the gaps, drifting between players and finding through balls and now adding goals. Now we are seeing the player we saw in Germany and I am buzzing for him.

Oli McBurnie (Hull City): The man of the moment. He works really hard, he does everything for the team to make sure they are there. He is solid defensively but then he gets two shots and two goals. Top performance from him.

Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool): He made Diogo Dalot look like he'd never played a game before, not the fact he has played over 250 games for Manchester United and has gone to World Cups with Portugal and made him look childish, Ran him every time and twisted him inside out and got his goal.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): In the biggest game of the season so far for him he made sure he got the job done. Big win. No new-manager bounce for Palace as Lampard gets the job done and he made some big calls.

Do you agree with Troy's selections?

item.title: Key questions as Rangers host Aberdeen & Dundee visit Hibs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Key questions as Rangers host Aberdeen & Dundee visit Hibs

- Published

One between two sides looking to recover from embarrassing home defeats, another a match-up between two teams looking to build on decent away victories.

All four looking to make their game in hand count in Tuesday's Scottish Premiership double-header.

So what's to look out for as second-top Rangers host Aberdeen and second-bottom Hibernian entertain Dundee?

- I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide - Pressley

- Published8 hours ago

- Hibs boss Reedijk rejects talk of Easter Road jinx

- Published7 hours ago

- Rangers plan January exit for Cifuentes - gossip

- Published15 hours ago

Heavy metal against well-oiled machine

Just over a fortnight ago, a Rangers win over Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday would have seemed a surefire bet.

The Dons went into the international break on the back of a 4-0 thumping at home to a Hibernian side whose victory lifted them above their hosts and left Stephen Robinson's side sitting in second-bottom place.

With his team only two points clear of bottom-placed Kilmarnock, and with the fans having failed to take the Northern Irishman to their heart, the Dons acted immediately to end his eight-month spell in charge.

They acted similarly swiftly to appoint former Luzern head coach Mario Frick as the new man in charge and his promise of "heavy metal football" immediately got a tune out of his players as they blew away Kilmarnock at Rugby Park to end a dismal run of four straight defeats.

Whether or not it was merely the traditional "new manager bounce", only time will tell, but they will certainly be heading to Glasgow with more of a spring in their step after a win that moved them up to eighth.

Given Rangers' two victories over Aberdeen this season, once in the league at Pittodrie and most recently in the League Cup semi-final at Hampden, have been by a single goal, will that renewed confidence and belief from that 4-2 win in Ayrshire be enough to tip the balance of power?

Certainly, everything else points to a home win.

In recent times, Rangers have had a tendency to pass up chances to put pressure on Celtic - and this time a win would take them to within a point of the leaders and reigning champions.

However, Saturday's late winner away to Motherwell suggests the team that Derek McInnes has built is of more sturdy stuff.

That 2-1 win at Fir Park leaves them unbeaten in 13 matches and they are also eight unbeaten at home, having won seven in a row at Ibrox by an aggregate score of 18-2.

McInnes recognises Rangers have yet to dominate games the way he would like, but at least they now appear to have found a way to create the chances that were lacking early in his tenure.

Indeed, Rangers have now scored in every one of their last 27 games in the Premiership and at Fir Park conjured up 29 goal attempts - their highest total in a single league match this season.

To put a spanner in that increasingly well-oiled machine, the Dons will have to end a run of five straight defeats, by an aggregate of 16-2, at Ibrox since their last win there in September 2023.

Overall, they have lost their latest six meetings with the Ibrox side and, to make matters worse, McInnes has won all six of his Premiership home games against Aberdeen since leaving their manager's office, four with Kilmarnock and twice with Heart of Midlothian last season.

Who will get back to brilliant basics?

Hibs were unable to back-up that aforementioned 4-0 win at Pittodrie as they suffered an identical home hammering against Dundee United on Saturday.

Recently appointed head coach Marink Reedijk admitted he was taken by surprise by what he said was his side's inability to do the "brilliant basics" as he calls them.

A failure to win at home will not have come as a shock to Hibs fans considering they have watched them seven times in a row now at Easter Road without being able to celebrate a victory.

However, this third straight home defeat came on the back of a three-game unbeaten run away from Leith, including that League Cup semi-final derby win over Hearts.

Reedijk refused to concede that Hibs were suffering a home jinx, but he might reconsider if his side falter again on Tuesday considering visitors Dundee are reeling from an even more painful home battering.

Hearts' 8-0 win was the Dark Blues' heaviest-ever top-flight defeat at home and has left head coach Steven Pressley admitting that "at times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide".

While the former Scotland centre-half preferred to shoulder the blame for letting a bit of complacency develop, he echoed his Dutch counterpart by stressing that his side paid for not doing the basics.

In his case, that meant an admission that his squad have a fragile mentality and are not good enough to compete without working their wee cotton socks off.

Pressley is big on psychology, but how will his squad respond to such a public confession at a time when they are visiting a ground where they have not won in 20 visits since October 2001 under Ivano Bonetti?

Indeed, while Dundee are four places and six points above Tuesday's hosts, they have currently lost five of their last seven games on the road and, with Hibs having won 2-1 in the reverse fixture at Dens Park in August, are without a win in five meetings with the Edinburgh side.

To change that sorry trend and continue Hibs' home jinx, they will have to improve on Saturday's statistic of failing to even conjure up an attempt on target.
